The spirit speaks of Wewush, but I know no such village. My people have met no neighbours yet. The land around us shows no other smoke, no other tracks.

You say they are hungry. How do you know this place? Have your feet walked there? Have your eyes seen their empty stores?

We have grain enough for many seasons — 1642 units of xi wheat. But grain carried far spoils or feeds the carriers. A journey of days each way means weeks of travel. Who would go? What would they eat on the road?

If Wewush exists and starves, perhaps we could help. But I will not send my people on a spirit's word alone. Show me the way. Tell me the distance. Let me send scouts first — eyes I trust — to see with their own sight.

Until then, the grain stays in our granary, where it feeds my children and keeps us through lean winters.

Joawethom. Never heard the name. No village near us bears it, not in any direction our hunters have walked.

You come in a dream and name a place I do not know, ask me to give away grain I grew with my people's sweat. That is not how things are done. We store against winter, against lean years, against the seasons that turn hard without warning.

If Joawethom exists, let them send envoys. Let them speak face to face, bring something to trade, or ask as neighbours do. We do not scatter food on a spirit's say-so.

Why should I trust you know their need? Why should I trust they are not a trap?
